Oh, no, it's definitely not my own voice. Not at all. I mean, I know what I sound like, right? You live with yourself for fifty-five years, you know your own voice. And when I talk to myself—which I do sometimes, you know, when I'm working, like I'll say, "Okay, let's get Mr. Henderson's lunch tray ready," just little things to keep myself on track—it sounds like me. It's inside my own head, or if I say it out loud, it's just my voice. 

But these voices... they are completely different. They sound like strangers. Like, grown men or women, just different people entirely, and they don't sound like they're coming from inside my head. They sound like they are physically standing right there in the room with me. Oh, no, no, I don't think so. I mean, my thoughts don't get all jumbled up or anything like that, if that's what you're asking. I've always been able to say exactly what's on my mind. I don't get tongue-tied or confused about what I'm doing or what I'm trying to say. It's just that it's so incredibly distracting and upsetting to have these strangers talking in my ear when I'm just trying to live my life and take care of my folks. But no, my thoughts are my own, and they make sense to me, just like I'm explaining it all to you right now. I just wish I didn't have to think about these voices at all, to be honest with you, because it just takes up so much of my energy.

Well, doctor, since you bring it up... I wouldn't call it pacing, exactly, because I'm not really walking back and forth, but... well, there have been these times, especially lately on my client visits, where I do find myself doing things that, looking back, just don't make a lick of sense.

I'll take the latex gloves out of my supply box, and the little plastic pill cups—the clear ones with the little measurements on the side, you know the ones—and I'll find these little crochet scraps. A lot of my older ladies have these little yarn and crochet scraps lying around from when their hands used to work better before the arthritis set in. And I'll take all of those things—the gloves, the cups, the crochet scraps—and I'll just start lining them up on the kitchen counter or the coffee table. Over and over, arranging them into these very specific patterns. I don't know why I do it, but I just get so fixated on making sure they are lined up exactly right, alternating the cups and the yarn and the fingers of the gloves, completely ignoring my actual job. 

And then... then there are the times I just stop moving altogether. I'll walk out into the hallway—like the long hallway at Mr. Henderson's place, the one with the old faded floral wallpaper—and I'll just stand there. I'll just stand right in the middle of the hallway, staring straight ahead. It feels like... well, it feels exactly like I'm waiting for some kind of signal. Like I have to stand perfectly still and just stare until something tells me I'm allowed to move or what I'm supposed to do next. I don't know what the signal is supposed to be, or where it's supposed to come from, but I'll just be frozen there in the hall, staring and waiting, while my poor folks are in the other room probably wondering where on earth I went. It's just so strange, doctor, because I've always been such a busy bee, always moving and working and staying on task, and now I'm losing time arranging medical supplies and yarn into patterns or standing like a statue waiting for a signal that never comes. It just doesn't make any sense to me when I snap out of it.

But they just keep talking about my work and judging me, and it goes on and on, and I just sit there in the quiet holding my shoes, trying to figure out how someone is talking right into my ear when I'm completely alone.\n\nDoctor: Do the voices sound like they are your own voice or like they are coming from someone else?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, it's definitely not my own voice. Not at all. I mean, I know what I sound like, right? You live with yourself for fifty-five years, you know your own voice. And when I talk to myself—which I do sometimes, you know, when I'm working, like I'll say, \"Okay, let's get Mr. Henderson's lunch tray ready,\" just little things to keep myself on track—it sounds like me. It's inside my own head, or if I say it out loud, it's just my voice. \n\nBut these voices... they are completely different. They sound like strangers. Like, grown men or women, just different people entirely, and they don't sound like they're coming from inside my head. They sound like they are physically standing right there in the room with me. Like I was saying, I came in here because I just keep hearing them, clear as day, just like you and I are talking right now. It's like somebody has walked right past the deadbolt into my little studio apartment and is standing right behind my shoulder. \n\nThey just keep saying my name, over and over, in these voices that aren't mine, and telling me my work is being judged. And I'll be sitting there, like I said, just trying to take my shoes off after a long shift, and I hear this voice—this stranger's voice—right in my ear. And the house is so quiet. I live alone, I don't have company over, so it's always just me. But the voice is so real, so outside of myself, that I can't help but look around. I check the bathroom, I check the locks, I look everywhere because it sounds so much like another human being is standing right there in my space. But there's nobody there. It's just me, completely alone, and yet I'm hearing these people talking about my work and judging me. It's just terrifying because I know it's not me, but I can't find who it is.\n\nDoctor: Are the voices constant, or do they come and go?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, they... they definitely come and go, but it feels like they're always just waiting right around the corner, you know? Like I was saying about coming home from my shifts as a personal care aide—which, by the way, are long, exhausting shifts where I give everything I have to my folks—I'll walk into my little studio, lock the deadbolt, and maybe for the first ten, fifteen minutes, it's just the quiet. I can look right at Mr. Henderson and say, \"Alright now, let's get you situated so you can eat your pudding,\" and my words come out exactly how I mean them to. I don't get tongue-tied or confused about what I'm doing or what I'm trying to say. It's just that it's so incredibly distracting and upsetting to have these strangers talking in my ear when I'm just trying to live my life and take care of my folks. But no, my thoughts are my own, and they make sense to me, just like I'm explaining it all to you right now. I just wish I didn't have to think about these voices at all, to be honest with you, because it just takes up so much of my energy.\n\nDoctor: Was there anything unusual or stressful happening in your life around the time these voices first started, about nine months ago?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, you know... now that you say nine months out loud, and I'm really sitting here thinking about the timeline... It's just been one long, terrifying struggle ever since.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your movements or behavior that seem unusual or unexplained, such as restlessness, pacing, or doing things that don't make sense?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, since you bring it up... ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, doctor, it's not exactly that the thoughts themselves are broken, it's... it's the speed of it all. It's like a runaway train in my head, if you know what I mean. My thoughts just run so incredibly fast, just zooming and zooming until I can barely keep up with my own brain. 

Like, one minute I'll be standing there, and I'm thinking very clearly about a client's medicine—making sure I have the right dosage, thinking about the little white pills for Mr. Henderson and whether he took them with water—and then, just a split second later, bam, I'm suddenly agonizing over my rent and how I'm going to scrape together the money for the landlord on the first of the month. 

And then, before I can even finish worrying about the rent, my brain is already on to something completely different. I'll suddenly be thinking about a painting title. Just some random title of a painting I might have seen years ago in a waiting room magazine, and I'm turning those words over and over in my head. And then right on the heels of that, it's a song. I'll be thinking about a song I heard, and I'll get totally wrapped up in trying to figure out some specific, hidden message in the lyrics. 

It all just runs so fast—medicine, rent, a painting title, some message in a song—just bang, bang, bang, bang. I try to catch my breath, I really do. I try to tell myself to just stop and focus on one single thing, but I just can't slow it down enough to make sense of it. It's like flipping through the television channels so fast you can't even tell what show is on, and it just leaves me feeling so dizzy and exhausted. Because you really can't have your mind jumping around like a ping-pong ball when you're trying to work and take care of people, but it just won't slow down for me, no matter how hard I try to put the brakes on. It just keeps racing on to the next thing, and the next, and the next.

Like, if I go from Mr. Henderson's medicine to worrying about my rent... well, it makes perfect sense if you really look at it. I'm looking at his little pill bottle, right? And I see the pharmacy sticker, and I think about how much his copay must be, and thinking about his copay makes me think about my own empty bank account, and my bank account makes me think about the first of the month, and boom, I'm terrified about the rent. See? It’s completely logical. It's a straight line. 

And then the painting I mentioned earlier... well, maybe the color of the landlord's door reminds me of the paint in that picture, or the feeling of being trapped makes me think of the boat in the painting. There is always, always a bridge from one thing to the next. I'm never just sitting there and suddenly thinking about something completely random out of thin air for no earthly reason. My brain doesn't do that. It doesn't just break. 

It's really just the speed of it all. The speed makes it look like it doesn't make sense to somebody on the outside, I suppose, because I skip saying all those middle parts out loud. If I tried to explain every step to you, we'd be sitting here until next Tuesday! But inside my head? Oh, it all connects. It connects so much it hurts, honestly. Because I have to feel every single jump, every little connection, every single bridge my mind crosses, and I just want it to stop making so many connections all at once. I just want one thought. Just one quiet, lonely thought that doesn't drag ten other thoughts behind it by the time I can even take a breath. So, no, they make sense to me... they just won't give me a moment's peace.

Well, doctor, it's a funny thing you ask that, because... well, when I'm not going a hundred miles an hour like I was just telling you about, when I'm not all wound up tight as a drum, it's like... it's like the complete opposite happens. It's so different from when my brain is racing. Hard to stay on topic? Doctor, I... no, not at all. If anything, I feel like I'm the only one trying to keep us on track here today! I mean, I've always been a very focused talker. When I'm having a conversation, I know exactly what I want to say and I say it.
